questions.s: Concerning the prevertebral fascia:
o: It extends inferiorly to the body of T3, the lower limit of longus colli

Last's says the prevertebral fascia is attached to the skull base in front of longus capitis and rectus capitis lateralis, extends down to the body of T3 (the lower limit of longus colli), and fades out laterally under trapezius.
Below T3 it blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament.
It is pierced by the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus

The four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (great auricular, lesser occipital, transverse cervical and supraclavicular) pierce the prevertebral fascia to reach the skin.
The motor branches stay deep to it.
The accessory nerve lies deep to it in the posterior triangle

The accessory nerve, the posterior triangle lymph nodes, the subclavian and axillary veins and the cervical sympathetic trunk lie anterior to (superficial to) the prevertebral fascia.
XI lies in the investing layer roof, so it is very superficial and easily injured in node biopsy.
It is prolonged over the subclavian artery into the axilla as the axillary sheath

The third part of the subclavian artery and the brachial plexus trunks lie behind the prevertebral fascia, so it is carried down over them into the axilla as the axillary sheath.
The subclavian vein lies in front of the fascia and is free to dilate.

questions.s: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia:
o: Forms the floor of the posterior triangle

The investing layer forms the roof of the posterior triangle. The floor is the prevertebral fascia over the muscles.
The accessory nerve runs within or just deep to the roof.
Splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius

The investing layer splits to enclose sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. It also splits to form the parotid capsule and the suprasternal space.
It is the outermost complete layer of deep fascia.
Is attached to the anterior tubercles of the cervical transverse processes

The anterior tubercles of the cervical transverse processes are related to the prevertebral fascia and the scalene muscles. The investing layer attaches to the skull, mandible, hyoid, ligamentum nuchae and pectoral girdle.
Different layers, different attachments.
Is attached to the hyoid bone

The investing layer is attached to the hyoid bone, which draws sternocleidomastoid forward in a gentle convexity.
It divides the front of the neck into suprahyoid and infrahyoid compartments.

questions.s: Regarding the pretracheal fascia and thyroid gland:
o: The pretracheal fascia is attached above to the hyoid bone and the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage

The pretracheal fascia is attached above to the hyoid bone and the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, and is limited laterally by the infrahyoid strap muscles.
It encloses the thyroid, trachea and oesophagus.
The fascia is firmly attached to the thyroid gland only between the isthmus and the second to fourth tracheal rings

The pretracheal fascia is firmly attached to the thyroid gland only between the isthmus and the second to fourth tracheal rings. Elsewhere the gland is loosely enclosed.
This attachment makes the thyroid (and its swellings) move up with swallowing.
Inferiorly the pretracheal fascia blends with the fibrous pericardium

Inferiorly the pretracheal fascia passes behind the brachiocephalic veins to blend with the adventitia of the aortic arch and the fibrous pericardium.
So infection in the pretracheal space can track into the mediastinum.
The sympathetic supply of the thyroid comes mainly from the inferior cervical ganglion

Last's says sympathetic fibres reach the thyroid from the superior cervical ganglion (with the superior thyroid artery) and the middle cervical ganglion (with the inferior thyroid artery).
The inferior (stellate) ganglion is not the main source.

questions.s: Concerning the carotid sheath and its contents:
o: The vagus nerve lies between and behind the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery

In the carotid sheath the vagus lies posteriorly in the gutter between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery, throughout the neck.
It is easily identified in carotid surgery.
The ansa cervicalis is embedded in the anterior wall of the sheath

The ansa cervicalis lies in (or on) the anterior wall of the carotid sheath, in front of the internal jugular vein.
It supplies the infrahyoid muscles.
The cervical sympathetic trunk lies within the sheath, medial to the vagus

The cervical sympathetic trunk lies behind the carotid sheath, outside it, on the prevertebral fascia.
That is why carotid sheath dissection does not usually cause Horner's syndrome.
The thoracic duct arches behind the left internal jugular vein at the level of C7

The thoracic duct arches up behind the left internal jugular vein (and carotid sheath) at the level of C7, then descends to the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins.
It can be injured in left supraclavicular surgery, causing a chyle leak.

questions.s: Tributaries of the internal jugular vein include the:
o: Inferior thyroid vein

The inferior thyroid veins drain into the brachiocephalic veins, not the internal jugular vein.
The superior and middle thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular.
Facial vein

The facial vein usually joins the internal jugular vein near the tip of the greater horn of the hyoid, often with the lingual and superior thyroid veins.
It is ligated in carotid surgery.
Vertebral vein

The vertebral vein drains into the brachiocephalic vein at the root of the neck, not the internal jugular.
It emerges from the transverse foramen of C6.
Inferior petrosal sinus

Last's says the inferior petrosal sinus is the first (highest) tributary of the internal jugular vein, joining just below the skull base.
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Regarding the external carotid artery:
o: It gives three branches from its front, two from behind and one from its medial side before entering the parotid

Before entering the parotid the external carotid gives three branches from its front (superior thyroid, lingual, facial), two from behind (occipital, posterior auricular) and one from its medial side (ascending pharyngeal).
The two terminal branches arise in the parotid.
It is separated from the internal carotid by the styloid process, stylopharyngeus and the glossopharyngeal nerve

The external and internal carotid arteries are separated by the styloid process, stylopharyngeus and IX, together with the stylohyoid ligament, the pharyngeal branch of X and the deep part of the parotid.
These structures pass between the two arteries.
The hypoglossal nerve crosses it deep to the internal jugular vein's facial tributary

XII runs superficial to the arteries but deep to the veins, including the facial vein.
So it lies sandwiched between the facial vein and the external carotid.
It ends behind the neck of the mandible by dividing into the maxillary and facial arteries

The external carotid ends in the parotid behind the neck of the mandible by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
The facial artery is an earlier branch from the front, below the mandible.

questions.t: Internal carotid artery in the neck
questions.s: The internal carotid artery in the neck:
o: Has no branches

The internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck.
That helps to distinguish it from the external carotid at operation.
Lies lateral to the external carotid at its origin

Last's says the internal carotid is lateral (external) to the external carotid at its origin, then slopes back to a more medial, deeper level.
The names refer to territory, not to position at the bifurcation.
Is crossed superficially by the hypoglossal nerve and the occipital artery

XII and the occipital artery cross the internal carotid superficially, as do the lingual and facial veins, and higher up the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid.
These must be retracted for high carotid exposure.
Has the superior laryngeal nerve passing superficial to it

The superior laryngeal nerve crosses obliquely behind (deep to) the internal carotid to reach its medial side, where it divides.
XII crosses superficially, the superior laryngeal deep.

questions.s: Concerning the carotid sinus and carotid body:
o: The carotid sinus is a dilatation at the origin of the internal carotid artery

The carotid sinus is a dilatation at the origin of the internal carotid artery. Its thin wall contains baroreceptors.
Pressure on it slows the heart and lowers blood pressure.
The carotid sinus is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve

The carotid sinus is supplied by IX through the carotid sinus nerve, which runs to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
It is the afferent limb of the baroreceptor reflex.
The carotid body lies behind the bifurcation of the common carotid artery

The carotid body lies behind the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. It contains chemoreceptor glomus cells and is supplied by IX and X.
Carotid body tumours (paragangliomas) splay the bifurcation.
The carotid body responds mainly to changes in blood pressure

The carotid body is a chemoreceptor, responding mainly to falling oxygen and rising carbon dioxide and acidity, and is concerned with respiratory reflexes. The sinus is the baroreceptor.
"Body = chemistry, sinus = pressure."

questions.s: Concerning the posterior triangle of the neck:
o: Its floor includes splenius, levator scapulae and the scalene muscles

The floor of the posterior triangle, from above down, is semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, levator scapulae, the three scalene muscles and the first digitation of serratus anterior.
All covered by prevertebral fascia.
The trunks of the brachial plexus lie behind the prevertebral fascia in its lower part

The trunks of the brachial plexus and the third part of the subclavian artery lie behind the prevertebral fascia in the lower part of the posterior triangle.
They can be blocked in the supraclavicular approach.
The cervical plexus lies within the posterior triangle

Last's says the cervical plexus lies on scalenus medius under cover of the upper sternocleidomastoid and does not actually lie in the posterior triangle. Only its cutaneous branches emerge into it.
The plexus is deep to the muscle.
The external jugular vein crosses it to pierce the investing fascia above the clavicle

The external jugular vein crosses the posterior triangle and pierces the investing fascia just above the clavicle, then drains into the subclavian vein.
If cut here it may be held open by the fascia and suck in air.

questions.s: Cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus and their roots:
o: Lesser occipital nerve, C3 and C4

The lesser occipital nerve is from C2 (anterior ramus). It hooks around the accessory nerve at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
C3 and C4 are wrong.
Great auricular nerve, C4 and C5

The great auricular nerve is from C2 and C3 (mainly C2).
It supplies the skin over the parotid and the lower ear.
Transverse cervical nerve, from the posterior ramus of C3

The transverse cervical nerve is from the anterior rami of C2 and C3 (cervical plexus). The third occipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C3.
Cervical plexus branches are all anterior rami.
Supraclavicular nerves, C3 and C4

The supraclavicular nerves come from C3 and C4 (mainly C4). Their medial, intermediate and lateral groups supply the skin down to the sternal angle and over the shoulder to the scapular spine.
C4 dermatome abuts T2 on the front of the chest.

questions.s: Regarding the ansa cervicalis:
o: Its superior root consists of C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve

The superior root of the ansa cervicalis consists of C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve. It was formerly called the descendens hypoglossi.
It leaves XII as the nerve crosses the internal carotid.
Its inferior root is formed from C2 and C3

The inferior root of the ansa is formed from C2 and C3 (formerly the descendens cervicalis). It spirals around the lateral side of the internal jugular vein.
It joins the superior root to form the loop.
It supplies thyrohyoid

Thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid) are supplied by C1 fibres directly from the hypoglossal nerve, not via the ansa.
The ansa supplies the other three strap muscles.
It supplies sternohyoid, omohyoid and sternothyroid

The ansa cervicalis supplies sternohyoid, omohyoid and sternothyroid. Segmentally, sternohyoid and omohyoid are C1 to C3 and sternothyroid C2 and C3.
The nerves enter the lower parts of the muscles, so high division of the straps preserves supply.

questions.s: Concerning scalenus anterior and its relations:
o: The phrenic nerve descends on its anterior surface deep to the prevertebral fascia

The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior, deep to the prevertebral fascia, crossing the muscle from lateral to medial.
This plastered position protects it in neck dissections that stay superficial to the fascia.
The subclavian vein passes behind it

The subclavian vein lies in front of scalenus anterior, superficial to the prevertebral fascia. The second part of the subclavian artery and the roots of the plexus lie behind it.
So the muscle separates vein from artery.
It arises from the anterior tubercles of C3 to C6 and inserts on the scalene tubercle of the first rib

Scalenus anterior arises from the anterior tubercles of C3 to C6 and inserts into the scalene tubercle of the first rib. It is supplied by C4 to C6.
It is the key landmark at the root of the neck.
The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries cross in front of it

The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries cross in front of scalenus anterior, superficial to the prevertebral fascia, between the muscle and the carotid sheath.
They are branches of the thyrocervical trunk.

questions.s: The pyramidal space between longus colli and scalenus anterior:
o: Has the carotid tubercle of C6 at its apex

The carotid (Chassaignac's) tubercle of C6 lies at the apex of the pyramidal space between longus colli and scalenus anterior.
It is a landmark for stellate ganglion block.
Contains the vertebral artery and vein

The pyramidal space contains the vertebral artery and vein and the inferior cervical (stellate) ganglion.
The vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen of C6 above it.
Has as its base the subclavian artery and neck of the first rib

The base of the space is formed by the subclavian artery and the neck of the first rib, with the suprapleural membrane between them.
The dome of the pleura lies just below.
Is roofed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia

Last's says there is no fascial roof across the pyramidal space.
So the investing layer is not its roof.

questions.s: Regarding the cervical sympathetic ganglia:
o: The superior cervical ganglion lies in front of the lateral masses of the atlas and axis

The superior cervical ganglion lies in front of the lateral masses of the atlas and axis, behind the carotid sheath and medial to the vertebral artery.
It is the largest cervical ganglion.
The superior ganglion gives grey rami to C1 to C4

The superior ganglion gives grey rami to C1 to C4. The middle gives grey rami to C5 and C6, and the inferior to C7 and C8.
There are no white rami in the neck.
The middle cervical ganglion lies medial to the carotid tubercle of C6, in front of the vertebral artery

Last's says the middle cervical ganglion is small and inconstant, lying medial to the carotid tubercle of C6 in front of the vertebral artery. The ansa subclavia passes in front of the subclavian artery to link it with the inferior (stellate) ganglion.
It is at risk in thyroid surgery near the inferior thyroid artery.
The stellate ganglion lies on the neck of the first rib

The stellate ganglion lies on the front of the neck of the first rib. Lateral to it, from medial to lateral, lie the supreme intercostal vein, the superior intercostal artery and the anterior ramus of T1.
Stellate block is done at C6 so the drug tracks down to it.

questions.s: Concerning the parotid gland:
o: From superficial to deep, the facial nerve, retromandibular vein and external carotid artery lie within it

Within the parotid the structures lie, from superficial to deep, as facial nerve, retromandibular vein and external carotid artery. The nerve lies immediately superficial to the vein, a surgical guide.
The plane of the nerve divides the gland into superficial and deep lobes.
Its secretomotor fibres relay in the otic ganglion

Secretomotor fibres to the parotid relay in the otic ganglion: inferior salivary nucleus, IX, tympanic branch, tympanic plexus, lesser petrosal nerve, otic ganglion, auriculotemporal nerve.
The auriculotemporal nerve also carries them to the gland.
Its fascia receives sensory fibres from the great auricular nerve

The parotid fascia receives sensory fibres from the great auricular nerve (C2, C3). The gland itself receives sensory fibres from the auriculotemporal nerve.
Swelling of the gland within its tight fascia is painful, as in mumps.
The parotid duct pierces masseter to open opposite the upper second premolar

The parotid duct crosses masseter, turns around its anterior border and pierces buccinator to open opposite the upper second molar.
It does not pierce masseter, and it is the molar, not the premolar.

questions.s: Regarding the maxillary artery:
o: It passes forward between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament

The maxillary artery passes forward between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament, with the auriculotemporal nerve above it and the maxillary vein below.
This is its first (mandibular) part.
Its first-part branches all enter bony foramina

The branches of the first part all enter bony foramina: inferior alveolar, middle meningeal, accessory meningeal, deep auricular and anterior tympanic.
Branches of the second part supply muscles; third-part branches go to the pterygopalatine fossa.
The accessory meningeal artery is an important supply to the trigeminal ganglion

Last's says the accessory meningeal artery enters through foramen ovale and runs up along the mandibular division as an important supply to the trigeminal ganglion.
It also supplies the dura nearby.
None of its branches pass through the petrotympanic fissure

The anterior tympanic artery passes through the petrotympanic fissure to the middle ear.
The deep auricular artery supplies the external meatus.

questions.s: The sphenomandibular ligament:
o: Is attached to the spine of the sphenoid and the lingula

The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula and lower margin of the mandibular foramen.
It is the remnant of the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage.
Is derived from the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage

The ligament is derived from the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage, a first-arch derivative.
The malleus and incus also come from this cartilage.
Is pierced by the nerve to mylohyoid

The nerve to mylohyoid (with its vessels) pierces the sphenomandibular ligament just above the mandibular foramen.
The vessels groove the mandible below.
Has the auriculotemporal nerve and maxillary artery passing between it and the neck of the mandible

The auriculotemporal nerve and maxillary artery pass between the ligament and the neck of the mandible. The inferior alveolar nerve and vessels pass between the ligament and the ramus.
All four statements are true: E.

questions.s: Concerning the muscles of mastication:
o: The posterior fibres of temporalis are the only fibres that retract the mandible

Last's says the posterior (horizontal) fibres of temporalis are the only fibres that retract the mandible; no other muscle retracts the condyle.
Lateral pterygoid protrudes it.
The masseteric nerve passes through the mandibular notch above the lateral pterygoid

The masseteric nerve passes laterally above lateral pterygoid and through the mandibular notch to enter masseter. It also supplies the temporomandibular joint (Hilton's law).
It is a branch of the anterior division.
The buccal nerve is the only branch to pass between the two heads of lateral pterygoid

The buccal nerve is the only branch to pass between the two heads of lateral pterygoid. It is sensory to the cheek, sometimes accompanied by a middle deep temporal nerve.
The nerve to masseter goes above the upper head.
Medial pterygoid is supplied by the anterior division of the mandibular nerve

Medial pterygoid is supplied from the main trunk of V3, which also gives the branch to the two tensors.
The anterior division supplies masseter, temporalis and lateral pterygoid.

questions.s: Regarding the temporomandibular joint:
o: It is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve and the nerve to masseter

The temporomandibular joint is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve (the main sensory supply) and the nerve to masseter, following Hilton's law.
Both are branches of V3.
Its articular surfaces are covered with hyaline cartilage

The articular surfaces of the joint are covered with fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage, because the mandible and squamous temporal bone ossify in membrane.
The sternoclavicular joint is the other classic fibrocartilage-covered joint.
The temporomandibular ligament is attached to the lateral surface of the articular tubercle

The temporomandibular (lateral) ligament is attached to the lateral surface of the articular tubercle and runs down and back to the neck of the mandible, deep to the parotid fascia.
It limits backward movement of the condyle.
It receives sensory branches from the facial nerve

The facial nerve is motor in this region and gives no sensory branches to the joint. Sensory supply is from V3 (auriculotemporal and masseteric nerves).
The facial nerve lies close to the joint but does not supply it.

questions.s: Regarding branches distributed through the pterygopalatine ganglion:
o: The nasopalatine nerve supplies the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum and the gum behind the incisors

The nasopalatine nerve passes through the sphenopalatine foramen, along the nasal septum and through the incisive canal. It supplies the posteroinferior part of the septum and the gum behind the incisors.
It is one of the nasal branches passing through the ganglion.
The greater palatine nerve supplies the whole hard palate except the incisor gum

The greater palatine nerve supplies the whole hard palate except the incisor gum, and also the posteroinferior lateral nasal wall.
It emerges through the greater palatine foramen.
The lesser palatine nerves supply the soft palate and tonsil

The lesser palatine nerves emerge through the lesser palatine foramina and supply the soft palate and tonsil.
They carry palatal taste fibres too.
The pharyngeal branch passes through the vomerovaginal canal

Last's says the pharyngeal nerve passes through the palatovaginal canal. The vomerovaginal canal transmits only a minute pharyngeal branch of the sphenopalatine artery.
Two similar-sounding canals; do not confuse them.

questions.s: The nerve supply of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity includes the:
o: Anterior ethmoidal nerve to the anterosuperior part

The anterior ethmoidal nerve, entering the nose through the slit beside the crista galli, supplies the anterosuperior part of the lateral wall (and septum).
It is a V1 branch.
Anterior superior alveolar nerve to the anteroinferior part

Last's says the anterior superior alveolar nerve reaches the anteroinferior quadrant of the lateral wall, including the region of the nasolacrimal duct.
It is a branch of the infraorbital nerve (V2).
Lateral posterior superior nasal nerves to the posterosuperior part

The lateral posterior superior nasal nerves, from the pterygopalatine ganglion through the sphenopalatine foramen, supply the posterosuperior part of the lateral wall.
The posteroinferior part is supplied by the greater palatine nerve.
Nasociliary branches of the facial nerve to the vestibule

The nasal vestibule is supplied by branches of the infraorbital nerve that have crept in from the face. The facial nerve has no nasociliary branches; nasociliary is a V1 nerve.
The statement mixes up two nerves.

questions.s: Concerning the wall of the pharynx:
o: The pharyngobasilar fascia is attached to the pharyngeal tubercle and the petrous temporal bone in front of the carotid canal

The pharyngobasilar fascia is attached to the pharyngeal tubercle and the petrous temporal bone in front of the carotid canal, then to the cartilaginous auditory tube and the medial pterygoid plate.
It fills the gap above the superior constrictor.
The cartilaginous auditory tube enters the nasopharynx above the upper border of the superior constrictor

The cartilaginous auditory tube enters the nasopharynx above the upper border of the superior constrictor, together with levator palati, through the gap between the skull base and the muscle.
Its opening is bounded by the tubal elevation.
Stylopharyngeus enters the pharynx between the middle and inferior constrictors

Stylopharyngeus, IX and the lingual nerve pass through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors.
The internal laryngeal nerve passes between the middle and inferior constrictors.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx deep to the lower border of the inferior constrictor

The recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx deep to the lower border of the inferior constrictor, just behind the cricothyroid joint, with the inferior laryngeal vessels.
The joint is a landmark in thyroid surgery.

questions.s: Muscles supplied by the pharyngeal plexus include:
o: Salpingopharyngeus

Salpingopharyngeus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus; all pharyngeal muscles except stylopharyngeus (IX) are supplied this way.
It descends from the auditory tube.
Palatopharyngeus

Palatopharyngeus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, the motor fibres arising in the nucleus ambiguus and reaching X via the cranial accessory root.
It forms the palatopharyngeal arch.
Levator veli palatini

Levator veli palatini is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus; all palatal muscles except tensor veli palatini (V3) are.
It elevates the soft palate.
The superior, middle and inferior constrictors

The three constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. Last's notes cricopharyngeus may also receive fibres from the recurrent or external laryngeal nerve.
All four true: E.

questions.s: Regarding tensor veli palatini:
o: It arises from the scaphoid fossa, the spine of the sphenoid and the cartilaginous auditory tube

Tensor veli palatini arises from the scaphoid fossa, the spine of the sphenoid and the cartilaginous auditory tube, so it arises outside the pharynx, from bone at front and back and cartilage between.
Its origin from the tube explains its role in opening it.
Its tendon turns around the pterygoid hamulus

Its tendon turns around the pterygoid hamulus and passes above the fibrous origin of buccinator to become the palatine aponeurosis.
The hamulus acts as a pulley.
It opens the auditory tube during swallowing

Tensor veli palatini opens the auditory tube during swallowing, with help from levator palati.
That is why swallowing equalises middle ear pressure.
It elevates the soft palate

Tensor veli palatini tenses the palatine aponeurosis, so that other muscles can elevate (levator palati) or depress it. It does not itself elevate the palate.
Levator elevates; tensor tenses.

questions.s: Concerning the development and innervation of the tongue:
o: Its muscles are derived from occipital myotomes, which explains the course of the hypoglossal nerve

The tongue muscles are derived from occipital myotomes. Their migration forward explains the course of XII, which passes outside the carotids but deep to the jugular vein.
That is why XII loops down into the neck before reaching the tongue.
The mucosa in front of the sulcus terminalis develops from the first arch

The mucosa in front of the sulcus terminalis develops from the first arch (tuberculum impar and lateral lingual swellings), supplied by the lingual nerve and chorda tympani.
So the anterior two-thirds has a first-arch general sensory nerve.
The second arch contributes most of the posterior third

Last's says the second arch is not represented in the tongue mucosa; the third arch overgrows it. IX supplies the posterior third, with a small fourth-arch area near the vallecula supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve.
So VII taste reaches the tongue only through the chorda tympani riding on a first-arch nerve.
The foramen caecum marks the origin of the thyroglossal duct

The foramen caecum, at the apex of the sulcus terminalis, marks the origin of the thyroglossal duct.
Thyroglossal cysts can lie anywhere along this track.

questions.s: Structures on the superficial (lateral) surface of hyoglossus include the:
o: Lingual nerve

On the lateral surface of hyoglossus, from above down, lie the lingual nerve, the submandibular duct and the hypoglossal nerve.
The lingual nerve loops around the duct here.
Lingual artery

The lingual artery lies deep to hyoglossus, with IX and the stylohyoid ligament.
The muscle separates the artery from XII.
Stylohyoid ligament

Last's says the stylohyoid ligament lies deep to hyoglossus, with IX and the lingual artery.
It runs to the lesser horn of the hyoid.
Glossopharyngeal nerve

IX passes deep to hyoglossus, at its posterior border.
Only the lingual nerve, duct and XII are superficial: answer A.

questions.s: Regarding the submandibular gland and duct:
o: The superficial and deep parts are continuous around the posterior border of mylohyoid

The superficial and deep parts of the submandibular gland are continuous around the posterior border of mylohyoid. The deep part lies between mylohyoid and hyoglossus.
Bimanual palpation feels the gland between finger in the mouth and hand on the neck.
The facial artery grooves the posterior part of the superficial part

The facial artery grooves the posterior part of the superficial part of the gland, then hooks over the mandible in front of masseter.
It must be ligated in submandibular gland excision.
The duct is about 5 cm long and opens beside the frenulum

The submandibular duct is about 5 cm long. It runs between mylohyoid and hyoglossus, then between the sublingual gland and genioglossus, and opens beside the frenulum on the sublingual papilla.
Stones are common here because the duct runs uphill.
The facial vein passes deep to the gland

The facial vein crosses the inferior (superficial) surface of the gland, with the cervical branch of VII and, if low, the marginal mandibular branch.
It does not pass deep to the gland.

questions.s: Concerning the larynx:
o: Its mucosa above the vocal folds is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve

The mucosa of the larynx above the vocal folds is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve; below the folds by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cell bodies of both are in the inferior vagal ganglion.
Aspiration above the cords triggers a cough via the internal laryngeal nerve.
The superior laryngeal artery is a branch of the superior thyroid artery

The superior laryngeal artery is a branch of the superior thyroid artery. It enters the larynx with the internal laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane.
The inferior laryngeal artery comes from the inferior thyroid.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds

Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds. It is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Bilateral recurrent nerve palsy can therefore cause airway obstruction.
The laryngeal cartilages derive from the second and third arches

The laryngeal cartilages derive from the fourth and sixth arches, not the second and third. Cricothyroid is a fourth-arch muscle (external laryngeal nerve).
The sixth arch gives the other intrinsic muscles (recurrent laryngeal nerve).

questions.s: The recurrent laryngeal nerve:
o: Supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
So recurrent palsy paralyses the abductor (posterior cricoarytenoid).
Lies immediately behind the cricothyroid joint

Last's describes the recurrent laryngeal nerve as lying immediately behind the cricothyroid joint; it is the joint with a nerve directly related to it.
The joint is the key landmark in thyroid surgery.
May divide into two branches before entering the larynx

Last's says the nerve is often double by the time it enters the larynx, having divided at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid isthmus.
Surgeons may mistake one branch for the whole nerve.
Is non-recurrent on the right when there is an aberrant right subclavian artery

With an aberrant (retro-oesophageal) right subclavian artery (1 to 2 percent), there is no artery for the right nerve to hook under, so it passes directly to the larynx.
A non-recurrent nerve is a hazard in thyroidectomy. All four true: E.

questions.s: Regarding the extraocular muscles:
o: Inferior oblique is the only extraocular muscle not arising from the back of the orbit

Inferior oblique is the only extraocular muscle that does not arise from the back of the orbit. It arises from the orbital floor beside the nasolacrimal canal.
The others arise from the common tendinous ring or near it.
The nerve to inferior oblique is the longest muscular nerve in the orbit

The nerve to inferior oblique is the longest muscular nerve in the orbit and carries the parasympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion.
A lesion of it can affect the pupil.
Superior oblique turns the eye down and out

Superior oblique turns the eye down and out (and intorts it).
Its main clinical action is depression of the adducted eye.
Lateral rectus is supplied by the abducent nerve entering its orbital surface

Last's says the nerves to the recti (and VI) enter the ocular surface of their muscles. Only IV enters its muscle (superior oblique) from the orbital surface.
So lateral rectus is entered on its deep (ocular) surface.

questions.s: The ciliary ganglion:
o: Contains synapses of sympathetic fibres to the dilator pupillae

Sympathetic fibres pass through the ciliary ganglion without synapse (they synapsed in the superior cervical ganglion), and dilator pupillae fibres travel mainly in the long ciliary nerves.
Only parasympathetic fibres synapse in the ganglion.
Receives its parasympathetic root from the superior division of the oculomotor nerve

The parasympathetic root comes from the nerve to inferior oblique, a branch of the inferior division of III.
The superior division supplies superior rectus and levator.
Sends sensory fibres to the conjunctiva

Last's says the sensory fibres from the ciliary ganglion supply the eye, cornea, iris and ciliary body, but not the conjunctiva, which is supplied by the nerves of the overlying lid.
A classic Last's detail.
Receives its sensory root from the nasociliary nerve

The sensory root of the ciliary ganglion comes from the nasociliary nerve; these fibres pass through without relay.
Answer D: 4 only.

questions.s: Concerning the ophthalmic artery and veins:
o: The central retinal artery is the first and smallest branch of the ophthalmic artery

Last's says the central retinal artery is the first and smallest branch of the ophthalmic artery, and also the most important. It is an end artery entering the inferomedial part of the optic nerve.
Occlusion causes sudden monocular blindness.
The ophthalmic artery crosses above the optic nerve from lateral to medial

The ophthalmic artery crosses above the optic nerve from lateral to medial, with the nasociliary nerve and the superior ophthalmic vein.
In the optic canal it was below and lateral.
The superior ophthalmic vein drains directly into the cavernous sinus

The superior ophthalmic vein drains directly into the cavernous sinus through the superior orbital fissure. It begins above the medial palpebral ligament, communicating with the angular vein.
This is the route of facial infection into the sinus.
The inferior ophthalmic vein drains only into the cavernous sinus

The inferior ophthalmic vein drains much of its blood through the inferior orbital fissure into the pterygoid plexus, as well as into the superior ophthalmic vein or cavernous sinus.
So it has two routes.

questions.s: Regarding the tympanic membrane:
o: It is set at about 55 degrees to the meatus, facing laterally, downwards and forwards

The tympanic membrane is set at about 55 degrees to the meatus, facing laterally, downward and forward. The umbo is produced by the tip of the handle of the malleus.
The cone of light is seen anteroinferiorly.
Its outer surface is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve and the auricular branch of the vagus

The outer surface of the tympanic membrane is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve and the auricular branch of the vagus; facial nerve fibres via the tympanic plexus may also reach it.
Vagal supply explains coughing on touching the drum.
Its inner surface is supplied by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve

The inner surface of the tympanic membrane is supplied by the tympanic branch of IX through the tympanic plexus.
The same plexus supplies the middle ear mucosa.
The chorda tympani crosses lateral to the neck of the malleus

The chorda tympani crosses medial to the neck of the malleus, over the pars flaccida, under the mucous membrane.
It lies on the inner side of the drum.

questions.s: Concerning the auditory tube:
o: Its bony part is longer than its cartilaginous part

The bony part of the auditory tube is about 1 cm and the cartilaginous part about 2 cm, the reverse of the external acoustic meatus.
So the cartilaginous part is longer.
The isthmus lies posteromedial to the spine of the sphenoid

The isthmus, the narrowest part of the tube at the junction of bony and cartilaginous parts, lies posteromedial to the spine of the sphenoid.
It is the commonest site of tubal obstruction.
It is derived from the second pharyngeal pouch

The auditory tube derives from the first pharyngeal pouch, with the middle ear and mastoid antrum.
The second pouch forms the tonsillar fossa.
Its cartilaginous part is supplied by the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve

Last's says the cartilaginous part is supplied by the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve (nervus spinosus), the bony part by the tympanic plexus (IX), and the ostium by the pharyngeal branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Regarding the mastoid antrum and suprameatal triangle:
o: The antrum lies about 15 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle

In the adult the mastoid antrum lies about 15 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle, which is bounded by the suprameatal spine and the upper and posterior tangents of the meatus.
It is the surgeon's surface landmark.
The antrum is present at birth

The mastoid antrum is present at birth, though the mastoid process and air cells develop later. Aeration of the process begins in the second year.
In infants the antrum is more superficial.
The lateral semicircular canal bulges into the medial wall of the aditus

The lateral semicircular canal bulges into the medial wall of the aditus to the antrum, just above the ridge of the facial canal.
It is a landmark in mastoid surgery.
The roof of the antrum is formed by the squamous temporal bone

The roof of the antrum is formed by the tegmen tympani of the petrous temporal bone, which also roofs the middle ear and the canal for tensor tympani.
Infection can erode it into the middle cranial fossa.

questions.s: Concerning the scalp:
o: Its vessels and nerves run in the dense connective tissue layer

The vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense connective tissue layer. The arteries are attached to the deep dermis, so they cannot retract and wounds bleed freely.
Bleeding is controlled by pressure against the skull.
Occipitalis arises from the highest nuchal line

Occipitalis arises from the highest nuchal line; only occipitalis has a bony attachment. Frontalis arises from orbicularis oculi and the skin of the eyebrows.
The two bellies are joined by the galea.
The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the anterior ramus of C2

The greater occipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C2. The lesser occipital nerve is from the anterior ramus of C2.
"Greater = posterior."
The supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries are branches of the internal carotid system

The supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery, so they belong to the internal carotid system.
They anastomose with branches of the external carotid on the scalp.

questions.s: Regarding the sensory supply of the face:
o: The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve

Last's says the skin over the angle of the mandible, supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), is the only facial skin not supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
This is why a V3 lesion does not numb the angle.
The zygomaticofacial nerve supplies the hairless skin of the temple

The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the hairless skin of the temple. The zygomaticofacial nerve supplies the skin over the zygomatic bone.
Both are branches of the zygomatic nerve (V2).
The infraorbital nerve supplies the upper lip and labial gum to include the second premolar

The infraorbital nerve supplies the upper lip and labial gum from the midline to include the second premolar.
The same "second premolar" rule applies to the mental nerve below.
The lower eyelid is supplied by the infratrochlear nerve

The lower eyelid and its conjunctiva are supplied by the palpebral branches of the infraorbital nerve. The infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial canthus area.
Upper lid V1, lower lid V2.

questions.s: Concerning venous connections of the face with the cavernous sinus:
o: The angular vein connects via the superior ophthalmic vein

The angular vein connects with the cavernous sinus through the superior ophthalmic vein. It is one of the two routes bounding Last's danger area.
The angular vein is the beginning of the facial vein.
The deep facial vein connects via the pterygoid plexus and emissary veins through foramen ovale

The deep facial vein connects with the cavernous sinus through the pterygoid plexus and emissary veins through foramen ovale (and the foramen of Vesalius, if present).
This is the second route.
The danger area lies below the level of the deep facial vein

Last's says the danger area (upper lip, nose and medial cheek) lies above the level of the deep facial vein, between the two communications.
Infections below that level drain safely down the facial vein.
Retrograde thrombosis of the inferior petrosal sinus and medullary veins is usually fatal

Last's says the ophthalmoplegia of cavernous sinus thrombosis is not itself dangerous; retrograde thrombosis of the inferior petrosal sinus and medullary veins is what is usually fatal.
Before antibiotics this was the cause of death.

questions.s: Concerning the branches of the facial nerve to the face:
o: Division of the zygomatic branches crossing the zygomatic arch can endanger vision

Division of the zygomatic branches crossing the zygomatic arch paralyses orbicularis oculi, so the lids cannot close. Corneal drying and ulceration then endanger vision.
Incisions over the arch are therefore made with care.
The marginal mandibular branch lies below the angle of the mandible in about 20%

The marginal mandibular branch lies below the angle and lower border of the mandible in about 20 percent of people.
That is why submandibular incisions are placed well below the mandible.
The buccal branches supply buccinator

The buccal branches supply buccinator; paralysis prevents emptying of the cheek pouch, so food collects there.
The buccal nerve of V3 is sensory only.
The cervical branch supplies the posterior belly of digastric

The cervical branch supplies platysma. The posterior belly of digastric is supplied by a branch given off just below the stylomastoid foramen.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
